aiStories.title: 要闻：构建一个用于演示的原型 AI Agent 与为 4000 万开发者实际运维一个 Agent，面临的是截然不同的工
aiStories.originalTitle: How Postman runs Agent Mode for 40 million developers on Amazon Bedrock
aiStories.source: AWS Machine Learning Blog (亚马逊云科技官方英文)
aiStories.snippet: Building an AI agent that works in a demo is a different problem from running one for 40 million developers. Postman and AWS share the architectural patterns behind Agent Mode: controlling tool sprawl, exposing schema-based reads, and treating context as the real bottleneck, plus how it runs on Amazon Bedrock at scale.
aiStories.fullContent:
Building an AI agent for a demo and operating one for 40 million developers are different engineering problems. Postman set out to build Agent Mode , an AI-native way to work across API testing , documentation , discovery, and implementation. The team expected model quality and prompt design to be the hardest problems. The deeper challenges came from integrating an agent into a mature product with years of interface-driven assumptions, a wide surface area, and specialized concepts.

In this post, Postman and AWS describe the architectural patterns that emerged while making a mature product legible to an AI agent. These patterns include controlling tool sprawl, exposing schema-based reads, and treating context rather than capability as the primary bottleneck.

We also explain how Agent Mode uses Amazon Bedrock for model flexibility, geographically scoped cross-Region inference, model-dependent zero data retention, and multi-tier prompt caching. Together, these lessons can help teams move production agents beyond prototypes.

Why Postman built Agent Mode

Agent Mode is Postman’s portal for working with the product in an AI-native way across testing, documentation, discovery, and implementation. Postman has evolved over 11 years, and developers and users learned to locate information through the interface by expanding sidebars, checking tabs, and opening requests. Re-engineering that awareness for an agent surfaced structural assumptions in the product’s APIs, user experience, and distribution of product knowledge. An agent reasons over data rather than navigating a screen. Figure 1 illustrates how Agent Mode works directly against the application.

Figure 1: Agent Mode works directly against the Postman application. In this example, it opens a pull request and proposes next steps without requiring the user to navigate through the interface

Agent Mode runs on Amazon Bedrock , which provides managed access to foundation models behind the agent. Supporting Postman’s global developer community creates variable, latency-sensitive demand with sharp traffic bursts. With Amazon Bedrock, Postman can scale this production workload without operating its own model-serving infrastructure while retaining flexibility in model selection and control over throughput, geographic processing, and cost. Figure 2 provides a high-level view of the production architecture before the following sections examine its components.

Figure 2: Postman Agent Mode combines client-side tools, agent orchestration, purpose-built context, and Amazon Bedrock model inference. Tools are scoped for each task, and user approval remains part of actions that modify application state

Human oversight is part of the production design. Agent Mode requires user approval before actions that modify application state. Postman also scopes available tools to the task, selects purpose-built context, and applies model-dependent data-retention settings. These controls reduce unintended actions and unnecessary data exposure, while production testing and monitoring remain necessary. As a responsible AI control, Postman uses Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to redact personally identifiable information before it reaches the underlying large language model (LLM). Enterprise admins can turn this on in Agent Mode’s guardrail settings.

In Agent Mode, tools define how the agent acts inside Postman. Early on, the team leaned toward highly atomic tools: small, precise actions such as opening a request, updating one field, or fetching a specific piece of metadata. That approach supported correctness and control in early iterations, but it also revealed several problems.

Many real-world workflows require long sequences of tool calls. Even when each step was fast, the overall experience felt slow, because every action had to return to the model before the next one could begin. Users watched the agent step through actions they had mentally grouped as a single operation.

In Postman’s testing, tool-selection errors increased once the visible toolset exceeded approximately 40 tools. The agent could call nonexistent tools, pass incorrect arguments despite valid schemas, or select tools that seemed semantically reasonable but were wrong in context. Larger or newer models reduced this behavior but didn’t remove it.

Past a certain toolset size, exposing more tools can reduce agent effectiveness. The current architecture selects tools based on need and context and isolates individual execution threads. The model sees only the tools relevant to the current task. Figure 3 illustrates this dynamic selection process.

Figure 3: The root agent queries a vector database of tool embeddings and narrows more than 170 tools to approximately 15 relevant to the request. It then hands those tools to a context-isolated sub-agent, so the model sees only the tools needed for the task

A subtler problem was that many client APIs were implicitly coupled to interface state. Tools that modified requests needed certain elements to be open, while other tools opened new tabs as side effects. The agent had to open a request tab to read it, mimicking interface interactions instead of reasoning about data. Postman is actively decoupling tools from tabs, and its Native Git feature makes extensive use of this approach. For example, Agent Mode can now send requests in the background without an open tab, although user approval is still required.

Builder takeaway: Treat your tool catalog as part of the context budget. Dynamically scope the tools exposed to the model per task, and decouple “what the agent can do” from “what the UI happens to have open.”

Exposing schema-based reads

For products such as the API Catalog, Postman consolidated multiple narrow views into a single query tool. These products expose structured data such as service uptime, test results, and endpoint response times across many services.

Given the schemas of the underlying ClickHouse tables, the agent can generate complex queries with joins and WHERE clauses. This substantially reduces the number of distinct tools needed to answer an analysis question:

SELECT toString(service_id) AS service_id, countMerge(total_events_state) AS total_requests, countMerge(error_events_state) AS total_errors, round(countMerge(error_events_state) * 100.0 / countMerge(total_events_state), 4) AS error_rate_pct, avgMerge(avg_latency_state) AS avg_latency_ms, quantileMerge(0.95)(p95_latency_state) AS p95_latency_ms FROM http_events_summary_1d WHERE service_id IN ('...list of service IDs') AND bucket_1d >= today() - 7 GROUP BY service_id HAVING p95_latency_ms < 100 AND total_requests > 0 ORDER BY error_rate_pct DESC;

With this approach, the engineering job shifts from building a tool per question to modeling the data well once . The agent can then generate a far wider variety of queries than the team could ever have enumerated as individual tools.

Builder takeaway: Where you have well-structured data, give the agent schema-aware read access to a query engine instead of a proliferation of single-purpose read tools. You trade tool count for data modeling, which produces a better scaling curve.

Context was the real bottleneck

Postman initially assumed missing tools would be the biggest blocker. In practice, missing or incomplete context caused more failures than missing capabilities.

Context is the agent’s understanding of where the user is in Postman, which entities are active, and what state has already been established. When that context was wrong or absent, even correct tools became ineffective. Figure 4 distinguishes the two forms of context supplied to the agent.

Figure 4: Two kinds of context feed the agent. Broad, shallow background context is gathered automatically and minified for the prompt. Deep, focused selected context is chosen by the user and routed through a dedicated handler for each entity type. Each handler distills the entity into the information the agent needs

The challenge was structural. Over 11 years, developers and users learned to find information through the interface. Re-engineering that awareness for an agent required multiple iterations to determine what mattered for each workflow and what was noise. Serializing the existing interface data model did not produce useful context because those objects were shaped for rendering and data transfer, not reasoning. Postman therefore built dedicated context handlers that distilled each entity into what the agent needed to know.

As more objects gained handlers, truncation became the next problem. Many fields contain open-ended user-generated data, including request descriptions, OpenAPI specifications, and request payloads. This data can crowd the context window. Managing the context budget carefully is essential at scale and supports the filesystem-backed approach the team is exploring, where each handler does not need custom truncation and expansion logic.

Builder takeaway: Don’t feed the model your rendering data model. Build purpose-shaped context handlers and treat the context window as a scarce, actively managed budget. Noise crowds out signal long before the model reaches its limit.

Putting it all together

As Agent Mode evolved, it became clear the system had to aggregate three distinct components, each solving a different problem.

Client-side tools live in the Postman application and represent the final actions the agent can take, such as opening requests, modifying settings, running collections, and inspecting authentication. Agent Mode also uses server-side tools for functions such as web search and agent-loop management, but most tools operate on the Postman application.

Generic agent instructions define system-level behavior, including how proactive Agent Mode should be, how it communicates uncertainty, and what baseline product knowledge it carries.

A knowledge base uses a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) approach. Postman has a large product surface that includes multiple request protocols, mock servers, monitors, documentation, the API Network, workspace governance, variables, helpers, code generation, request settings, and collection runs.

Encoding all of this in static prompts was not feasible, and most of it is irrelevant to a given query. For initial seeding, the team used Postman’s Learning Center to generate concise feature-specific articles. At runtime, Agent Mode selects knowledge articles based on the incoming query and available context. For example, when a user selects a mock server, Agent Mode injects the related article automatically. This keeps the agent lightweight by default while providing depth when needed. The knowledge base evolves with the application, so teams can ship Agent Mode documentation with new features.

Running Agent Mode on Amazon Bedrock

The three components previously described resolve to the same runtime action: an inference call to a foundation model (FM). At Postman’s scale, traffic is bursty and developer-driven. Routing, caching, and geographic processing controls help Postman accommodate traffic bursts, manage inference cost, and address workload-specific processing requirements. Amazon Bedrock provides four capabilities that matter most here.

Model flexibility across the Claude family

Agent Mode isn’t tied to one model. Through Amazon Bedrock model inference APIs , Postman can access supported Anthropic Claude models and route each workload to an appropriate model. A faster model can serve high-volume, latency-sensitive interactions, while a larger model can handle complex reasoning where quality matters more than cost. Moving between supported Claude models is primarily a configuration change rather than a new integration. This flexibility directly supports the tool-sprawl and context challenges described earlier. In Postman’s testing, newer and larger models reduced tool hallucinations, and Postman can adopt supported models without rebuilding the integration. See supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock .

Cross-Region inference for high throughput

Developer traffic is spiky, and provisioning for peak demand in one AWS Region can be costly. Agent Mode uses Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference to automatically route requests among the destination Regions defined by an inference profile. At runtime, the application passes the selected inference profile ID or Amazon Resource Name (ARN) as the modelId in Converse or InvokeModel. The profile, applicable AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and service control policies, and quotas must permit every destination Region that Bedrock might select.

Geographic inference profiles route requests only among supported Regions within a defined geography, such as the United States or European Union. This option combines increased throughput with a configured geographic processing boundary.

Global inference profiles can route requests among supported destination Regions worldwide to provide additional throughput during traffic bursts. They are appropriate only when the workload does not require a geographically constrained processing boundary.

Postman can select the inference profile per workload: a global profile for maximum available throughput or a geographic profile when processing must remain within the profile’s defined geography. This choice is explicit in the modelId used for each Bedrock inference request.

# Schematic Converse request response = bedrock_runtime.converse( modelId="<geographic-inference-profile-id-or-arn>", messages=messages, system=system_blocks, )

Data residency and enterprise controls

For enterprise customers, permitted processing geography can be as important as throughput. Geographic inference profiles constrain Bedrock routing to the profile’s supported destination Regions within the selected geography. This does not mean that inference runs inside Postman’s own AWS environment. Amazon Bedrock processes requests in the eligible AWS Regions for that profile, with data encrypted in transit and at rest. AWS states that Bedrock doesn’t use prompts and completions to train AWS models or distribute them to third parties. Postman has configured zero data retention with data_retention_mode set to none for supported Agent Mode models. Availability and behavior are model-dependent, so each production model must be checked against the current Amazon Bedrock data-protection and retention documentation .

Prompt caching to keep costs in check

A production agent resends substantial stable context on each turn, including system instructions, generic agent behavior, a core tool set, selected knowledge, and conversation context. Reprocessing the unchanged prefix on every request adds avoidable latency and cost.

Agent Mode uses Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to reuse stable prompt prefixes. The near-immutable core, including the system prompt, agent instructions, and core tool definitions, uses a one-hour cache checkpoint. More variable context uses a five-minute checkpoint that refreshes on a cache hit. Bedrock requires the longer-lived checkpoint to appear before the shorter-lived checkpoint. The shorter tier suits interactive sessions because idle context expires, while the one-hour tier can amortize its higher cache-write price across many reads. Cache benefits and supported TTLs depend on the selected model. Teams can verify behavior through the cacheReadInputTokens and cacheWriteInputTokens usage fields and measure time to first token for their own workloads.

# Schematic cache checkpoints in Converse content blocks {"cachePoint": {"type": "default", "ttl": "1h"}} # stable core {"cachePoint": {"type": "default", "ttl": "5m"}} # variable layer

Builder takeaway: Treat inference as a routing-and-caching problem, not only a model-selection decision. Select the Claude model per workload, choose the appropriate cross-Region inference profile, and cache the stable prompt prefix with TTLs that match how frequently each layer changes.

Best practices for scaling agents in production

Distilled from Postman’s journey, for builders working on Amazon Bedrock:

Budget tools as carefully as tokens. Dynamically select the tools exposed per task. In Postman’s testing, tool-selection errors increased as the visible toolset became large.

Prefer schema-aware reads over tool proliferation. Model your data well and let the agent query it.

Decouple agent actions from interface state. If a tool requires an open tab, the agent is navigating the interface rather than reasoning directly over data.

Engineer context deliberately. Purpose-built context handlers beat serializing your rendering model every time.

Manage the context window as a scarce resource. Truncation and expansion strategy is a first-class design problem, not an afterthought.

Ship docs with features. A RAG knowledge base only stays useful if it evolves in lockstep with the product.

Route and cache on Bedrock. Match each workload to the appropriate Claude model, choose cross-Region inference based on throughput and geographic requirements, and apply tiered caching to stable prompt prefixes.

Building Agent Mode required Postman to confront the gap between large language model capabilities and the structure of mature products: interface assumptions, coupled clients, sprawling tool catalogs, and knowledge distributed across documentation and teams. Dynamic tool selection, schema-based reads, and deliberate context engineering emerged as repeatable patterns at the scale of Postman’s developer community . Amazon Bedrock provides the managed model access, cross-Region inference , model-dependent retention controls , and prompt caching that support the production architecture.

Whether you’re building your first agent or scaling an existing one, these patterns can help teams avoid common agent-integration and scaling challenges.

To learn more, see the Amazon Bedrock documentation , including guidance for cross-Region inference , prompt caching , and data protection and retention . For related implementation guidance, read Effectively use prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock announces global cross-Region inference for increased throughput on the AWS Machine Learning Blog. To explore the product, see the Postman Agent Mode documentation .

Postman’s production implementation is proprietary and isn’t available as a public sample repository.

Srinivas is a Senior Engineer on Postman’s AI team, building enterprise agents at the intersection of distributed systems and AI infrastructure. His focus is core agent architecture that keeps agents reliable and accurate at scale.

Shubham is a Solutions Architect at AWS based in Bengaluru, India, supporting independent software vendors (ISVs). He works with engineering and leadership teams to design, build, and run their products on AWS, from first architecture to production, with a deep focus on generative AI and resilience at scale. Outside of work, Shubham is an avid hiker who brings the same preparation and persistence from the trail to building systems that last.
aiStories.fullTranslation:
构建一个用于演示的原型 AI Agent 与为 4000 万开发者实际运维一个 Agent，面临的是截然不同的工程问题。Postman 着手打造了 Agent Mode，这是一种贯穿 API 测试、文档、发现和实现的 AI 原生工作方式。团队最初预计模型质量和提示词设计会是最棘手的问题，但更深层次的挑战实际上来自于将 Agent 集成到一个成熟的产品中——该产品承载着多年基于界面的设计假设、庞大的功能覆盖面以及专业化的概念。

在这篇文章中，Postman 与 AWS 介绍了在使成熟产品能够被 AI Agent 充分理解的过程中所总结出的架构模式。这些模式包括：控制工具泛滥（tool sprawl）、提供基于 Schema 的读取接口，以及将上下文而非模型能力视为核心瓶颈。

我们还将解释 Agent Mode 如何利用 Amazon Bedrock 实现模型灵活性、受地理范围限制的跨区域推理、基于模型的零数据保留（zero data retention）以及多层级提示词缓存（multi-tier prompt caching）。综合这些经验，可以帮助各团队推动生产级 Agent 超越原型阶段。

为什么 Postman 构建 Agent Mode

Agent Mode 是 Postman 的核心入口，让用户能够以 AI 原生方式在测试、文档、发现和实现等全流程中使用该产品。Postman 经过了 11 年的发展演进，开发者和用户早已习惯通过界面查找信息：展开侧边栏、切换选项卡以及打开请求。要为 Agent 重构这种感知能力，暴露出产品在 API、用户体验以及产品知识分布方面的结构性假设。Agent 是针对数据进行推理，而非在屏幕上导航。图 1 展示了 Agent Mode 如何直接与应用程序交互协同。

图 1：Agent Mode 直接针对 Postman 应用程序工作。在此示例中，它创建了一个拉取请求（pull request）并提出后续步骤建议，无需用户在界面中手动导航。

Agent Mode 运行在 Amazon Bedrock 之上，后者为 Agent 背后的基础模型提供托管式访问。为 Postman 的全球开发者社区提供支持，带来了多变且对延迟高度敏感的需求，同时伴随急剧的流量突发。借助 Amazon Bedrock，Postman 可以在无需自行运维模型服务基础设施的情况下扩展该生产工作负载，同时保留了模型选择的灵活性，并对吞吐量、地域处理与成本拥有掌控力。图 2 提供了生产架构的高级概览，随后的章节将深入剖析其各个组件。

图 2：Postman Agent Mode 结合了客户端工具、Agent 编排、定制化上下文以及 Amazon Bedrock 模型推理。工具按任务进行范围界定，而在修改应用程序状态的操作中，用户审批始终是必经环节。

人工监督是生产设计的重要组成部分。Agent Mode 在执行修改应用程序状态的操作之前需要获得用户批准。Postman 还会根据任务限定可用工具的范围，挑选定制的上下文，并应用基于模型的数据保留策略设置。这些控制措施减少了非预期操作与不必要的数据暴露，与此同时生产环境的测试与监控仍然必不可少。作为负责任的 AI（Responsible AI）管控举措，Postman 使用 Amazon Bedrock Guardrails（护栏）在个人身份信息（PII）到达底层大语言模型（LLM）之前将其脱敏。企业管理员可在 Agent Mode 的护栏设置中开启此功能。

在 Agent Mode 中，工具定义了 Agent 在 Postman 内部的具体操作方式。早期，团队倾向于采用高度原子化的工具：微小且精确的动作，例如打开请求、更新一个字段或获取特定元数据。这种方式在早期迭代中保证了正确性和可控性，但同时也暴露出若干问题。

许多现实工作流需要较长的工具调用序列。即使每一步都很快，整体体验依然显得缓慢，因为每个动作都必须先返回给模型，然后才能开始下一步。用户不得不看着 Agent 逐步执行那些在人类思维中本已归类为单一操作的动作。

在 Postman 的测试中，一旦可见工具集超过大约 40 个，工具选择错误的概率就会上升。Agent 可能会调用不存在的工具，即使 Schema 有效也会传递错误的参数，或者选择语义上看起来合理但在上下文中并不正确的工具。更大或更新的模型缓解了这种行为，但并未完全消除。

超过一定工具集规模后，暴露更多工具反而会降低 Agent 的有效性。当前架构根据需求和上下文动态选择工具，并隔离各个独立的执行线程。模型只能看到与当前任务相关的工具。图 3 说明了这一动态选择过程。

图 3：Root Agent 查询工具嵌入（embeddings）的向量数据库，将 170 多个工具缩小到与请求相关的约 15 个。然后将这些工具移交给上下文隔离的 Sub-Agent，以便模型仅能看到当前任务所需的工具。

一个更隐蔽的问题是，许多客户端 API 隐式地与界面状态耦合。修改请求的工具需要特定界面元素处于打开状态，而其他工具则会附带打开新标签页的副作用。Agent 必须先打开一个请求标签页才能读取它，这实际上是在模仿界面交互，而不是针对数据进行推理。Postman 正在积极将工具与标签页解耦，其原生 Git 功能广泛应用了这一方法。例如，Agent Mode 现在可以在没有打开标签页的情况下在后台发送请求，尽管这仍然需要用户批准。

开发者启示：将工具目录视作上下文预算（context budget）的一部分。按任务动态限定向模型暴露的工具范围，并将“Agent 能做什么”与“UI 当前恰好打开了什么”解耦开来。

提供基于 Schema 的读取接口

对于诸如 API Catalog 这类产品，Postman 将多个狭窄的视图整合为一个统一的查询工具。这些产品对外提供跨多个服务的结构化数据，例如服务正常运行时间、测试结果以及端点响应时间。

在获得底层 ClickHouse 表的 Schema 后，Agent 可以生成带有 JOIN 和 WHERE 子句的复杂查询。这大幅减少了回答分析类问题所需的独立工具数量：

SELECT toString(service_id) AS service_id, countMerge(total_events_state) AS total_requests, countMerge(error_events_state) AS total_errors, round(countMerge(error_events_state) * 100.0 / countMerge(total_events_state), 4) AS error_rate_pct, avgMerge(avg_latency_state) AS avg_latency_ms, quantileMerge(0.95)(p95_latency_state) AS p95_latency_ms FROM http_events_summary_1d WHERE service_id IN ('...list of service IDs') AND bucket_1d >= today() - 7 GROUP BY service_id HAVING p95_latency_ms 0 ORDER BY error_rate_pct DESC;

借助这种方法，工程重心的工作从“为每个问题构建一个工具”转变为“对数据做好一次性建模”。这样，Agent 便能生成种类远比团队手工罗列单个工具丰富得多的查询。

构建者心得：如果你拥有结构良好的数据，应当为智能体提供对查询引擎的感知架构模式（schema-aware）的读取访问权限，而不是去堆积大量单一用途的读取工具。你是在用数据建模来换取工具数量的减少，这会带来更优的扩展曲线。

上下文才是真正的瓶颈

Postman 最初以为缺少工具会是最大的阻碍。但在实践中，缺失或不完整的上下文所导致的失败，远多于缺失功能所导致的失败。

上下文是指智能体对用户在 Postman 中所处位置、哪些实体处于活动状态以及已经建立了何种状态的理解。当该上下文错误或缺失时，即便是正确的工具也会变得无效。图 4 区分了提供给智能体的两种形式的上下文。

图 4：向智能体输入两种上下文。广泛、浅层的背景上下文由系统自动收集并针对提示词进行了精简。深入、聚焦的选定上下文由用户选取，并通过针对每种实体类型的专用处理器进行路由。每个处理器将实体提炼为智能体所需的信息。

这一挑战源自结构层面。在过去的 11 年里，开发者和用户习惯于通过界面来寻找信息。要为智能体重新构建这种感知能力，需要经历多次迭代，以确定在每个工作流程中哪些信息重要、哪些是噪声。直接序列化现有的界面数据模型并不能产生有用的上下文，因为这些对象的组织方式是为了渲染和数据传输，而不是为了推理。因此，Postman 构建了专用的上下文处理器，将每个实体提炼为智能体需要知道的信息。

随着越来越多的对象拥有了专用处理器，截断成为了下一个问题。许多字段包含开放式的用户生成数据，包括请求描述、OpenAPI 规范和请求载荷。这些数据可能会挤占上下文窗口。在大规模场景下，审慎管理上下文预算至关重要，这也支持了团队正在探索的基于文件系统的方法，使每个处理器无需编写自定义的截断和扩展逻辑。

构建者心得：切勿将你的渲染数据模型直接投喂给模型。应构建契合目标用途的上下文处理器，并将上下文窗口视为稀缺且需要主动管理的预算。早在模型达到其容量上限之前，噪声就会淹没有效信号。

综合集成

随着 Agent Mode 的演化，系统必须聚合三个不同的组件，且每个组件解决不同的问题，这一点变得越发清晰。

客户端工具存在于 Postman 应用程序中，代表了智能体可以执行的最终操作，例如打开请求、修改设置、运行集合和检查身份验证。Agent Mode 还会将服务端工具用于网络搜索和智能体循环管理等功能，但大多数工具都直接作用于 Postman 应用程序。

通用智能体指令定义了系统层面的行为，包括 Agent Mode 应当有多主动、它如何传达不确定性，以及它具备哪些基线产品知识。

知识库采用检索增强生成（RAG）方法。Postman 拥有庞大的产品功能面，包括多种请求协议、Mock 服务器、监视器、文档、API 网络、工作区治理、变量、辅助函数、代码生成、请求设置和集合运行。

将所有这些内容硬编码到静态提示词中是不可行的，而且对于特定的查询而言，其中大部分内容都是无关的。为了进行初始数据填充，团队利用 Postman 的学习中心生成了针对具体功能的简明文章。在运行时，Agent Mode 会根据传入的查询和可用上下文选择知识文章。例如，当用户选择某个 Mock 服务器时，Agent Mode 会自动注入相关的文章。这使智能体在默认状态下保持轻量，同时在需要时能够提供深度信息。知识库会随应用程序一同演进，因此各团队可以在交付新功能的同时发布对应的 Agent Mode 文档。

在 Amazon Bedrock 上运行 Agent Mode

前文所述的三个组件在运行时都归结为相同的操作：对基础模型（FM）发起推理调用。在 Postman 的规模下，流量呈现出突发性且由开发者行为驱动。路由、缓存和地理处理控制有助于 Postman 应对流量突增、管理推理成本并满足针对特定工作负载的处理要求。Amazon Bedrock 提供了在此场景下最重要的四项功能。

Claude 家族内的模型灵活性

Agent Mode 并不绑定于单一模型。通过 Amazon Bedrock 模型推理 API，Postman 可以访问受支持的 Anthropic Claude 模型，并将每个工作负载路由到合适的模型。更快的模型可以服务于大吞吐量、延迟敏感的交互，而更大的模型可以处理复杂推理——此时质量重于成本。在受支持的 Claude 模型之间切换主要属于配置变更，无需重新进行集成。这种灵活性直接支持了前述的工具蔓延和上下文挑战。在 Postman 的测试中，更新、更大的模型减少了工具调用的幻觉，而且 Postman 无需重新构建集成即可采用受支持的新模型。请参阅 Amazon Bedrock 各 AWS 区域受支持的模型。

用于实现高吞吐量的跨区域推理

开发者流量往往具有突发尖峰，在一个 AWS 区域内为峰值需求预置资源可能会成本高昂。Agent Mode 使用 Amazon Bedrock 跨区域推理，在推理配置文件所定义的目标区域之间自动路由请求。在运行时，应用程序将所选推理配置文件的 ID 或亚马逊资源名称（ARN）作为 modelId 传递给 Converse 或 InvokeModel。该配置文件、适用的 AWS 身份与访问管理（IAM）和服务控制策略以及配额必须允许 Bedrock 可能选中的每个目标区域。

地理推理配置文件仅在指定地理区域（例如美国或欧盟）内受支持的区域之间路由请求。该选项将提高吞吐量与配置的地理处理边界相结合。

全球推理配置文件可以在全球受支持的目标区域之间路由请求，以便在流量突发期间提供额外的吞吐量。仅当工作负载不需要受到地理约束的处理边界时，才适合使用该选项。

Postman 可以按工作负载选择推理配置文件：需要最大可用吞吐量时选择全球配置文件，而当处理必须保留在配置文件定义的地理区域内时选择地理配置文件。这一选择明确体现在用于每个 Bedrock 推理请求的 modelId 中。

# Converse 请求示意代码
response = bedrock_runtime.converse(
    modelId=" ",
    messages=messages,
    system=system_blocks,
)

数据驻留与企业级控制

对于企业客户而言，获准的数据处理地理位置可能与吞吐量同样重要。地理推理配置文件（Geographic inference profiles）将 Bedrock 的路由限制在所选地理区域内该配置文件支持的目的区域。这并不意味着推理运行在 Postman 自身的 AWS 环境内部。Amazon Bedrock 会在该配置文件适用的 AWS 区域中处理请求，且数据在传输和静态存储状态下均经过加密。AWS 声明，Bedrock 不会使用提示词和补全内容来训练 AWS 模型，也不会将其分发给第三方。针对支持的 Agent 模式模型，Postman 已将 data_retention_mode 设置为 none，从而配置了零数据保留。可用性和具体行为取决于模型，因此必须对照当前 Amazon Bedrock 数据保护与保留文档来核验每个生产模型。

提示词缓存以控制成本
生产级 Agent 在每一轮交互中都会重新发送大量稳定的上下文，包括系统指令、通用 Agent 行为、核心工具集、精选知识和对话上下文。在每次请求中重复处理未改变的前缀会带来可以避免的延迟和成本。

Agent 模式使用 Amazon Bedrock 提示词缓存（prompt caching）来复用稳定的提示词前缀。近乎不变的核心部分（包括系统提示词、Agent 指令以及核心工具定义）采用 1 小时的缓存检查点。更易变的上下文则采用 5 分钟的检查点，该检查点在命中缓存时刷新。Bedrock 要求生存期更长的检查点必须出现在生存期较短的检查点之前。较短的层级适用于交互式会话，因为空闲上下文会自动过期；而 1 小时的层级则可以通过多次读取来分摊其较高的缓存写入成本。缓存收益和受支持的 TTL（生存时间）取决于所选模型。各团队可以通过 cacheReadInputTokens 和 cacheWriteInputTokens 使用率字段来验证其行为，并针对自身的工作负载测量首字元生成时间（time to first token）。

# Converse 内容块中的示意性缓存检查点
{"cachePoint": {"type": "default", "ttl": "1h"}} # 稳定核心
{"cachePoint": {"type": "default", "ttl": "5m"}} # 可变层

构建者心得：将推理视为一个“路由与缓存”问题，而不仅仅是一个模型选择决策。根据工作负载选择具体的 Claude 模型，选用恰当的跨区域推理配置文件，并使用与各层变更频率相匹配的 TTL 来缓存稳定的提示词前缀。

在生产环境中扩展 Agent 的最佳实践
从 Postman 的实践历程中提炼出以下供 Amazon Bedrock 构建者参考的建议：

像把控 Token 预算一样严格规划工具预算。按任务动态筛选暴露的工具。在 Postman 的测试中，随着可见工具集规模变大，工具选择错误的发生率也随之上升。
优先选择感知 Schema 的读取，而非让工具数量泛滥。妥善建模你的数据，并让 Agent 查询它。
将 Agent 操作与界面状态解耦。如果一个工具要求打开特定选项卡，那么 Agent 实际上是在浏览界面，而不是直接对数据进行推理。
精心设计上下文工程。专用的上下文处理器每一次都优于将渲染模型直接序列化的做法。
将上下文窗口视为稀缺资源进行管理。截断和扩展策略是一等设计问题，而非事后补救。
文档随功能一同交付。只有与产品保持同步演进，RAG 知识库才能持续发挥价值。
在 Bedrock 上进行路由与缓存。将各工作负载与相匹配的 Claude 模型对应起来，根据吞吐量和地理合规要求选择跨区域推理，并对稳定的提示词前缀应用分层缓存。

构建 Agent 模式需要 Postman 直面大语言模型能力与成熟产品架构之间的差距：界面假设、耦合的客户端、野蛮生长的工具目录，以及分散在文档和各个团队中的知识。在 Postman 庞大的开发者社区规模下，动态工具选择、基于 Schema 的读取和深思熟虑的上下文工程成为了经过验证的可复用模式。Amazon Bedrock 提供了托管模型访问、跨区域推理、依赖模型的数据保留控制以及提示词缓存，为这一生产架构提供了坚实支撑。

无论你是正在构建第一个 Agent，还是正在扩展现有的 Agent，这些模式都可以帮助团队避免常见的 Agent 集成与扩展难题。

如需了解更多信息，请参阅 Amazon Bedrock 文档，包括关于跨区域推理、提示词缓存以及数据保护与保留的指南。相关实施指导请阅读 AWS Machine Learning Blog 上的《在 Amazon Bedrock 上有效使用提示词缓存》以及《Amazon Bedrock 宣布推出全局跨区域推理以提高吞吐量》。如需探索该产品，请参阅 Postman Agent 模式文档。

Postman 的生产实现属于专有技术，不作为公开示例代码库提供。

Srinivas 是 Postman AI 团队的高级工程师，致力于在分布式系统与 AI 基础设施的交叉领域构建企业级 Agent。他的研究重点是确保 Agent 在规模化环境下保持可靠与准确的核心 Agent 架构。

Shubham 是常驻印度班加罗尔的 AWS 解决方案架构师，主要支持独立软件开发商（ISV）。他与工程和领导团队合作，在 AWS 上设计、构建和运行其产品（从最初的架构搭建到正式投入生产），并深入专注于生成式 AI 和大规模弹性。在工作之余，Shubham 是一位狂热的徒步爱好者，他将步道上的充分准备与坚韧精神同样倾注于构建持久稳固的系统之中。

aiStories.title: 面向GPU集群的高影响力调度
aiStories.originalTitle: Impactful scheduling for GPU clusters
aiStories.fullContent:
On the AI Infrastructure team at Ai2, we’re responsible for providing the institute’s GPU compute capacity, specifically targeting large, distributed training workloads. We think about this task as a pyramid of four metrics that build on each other.

The foundation is availability: how often the hardware is healthy and ready for work. Above this is occupancy: the fraction of available time assigned to a specific workload. Next is impact: how often the most valuable workloads are chosen to receive resources. The capstone of the pyramid is utilization: the fraction of GPU capacity used over the lifetime of a workload.

This post is about improving the impact of our scheduling decisions. We recently replaced a priority-based scheduler with a system including GPU time budgets, hierarchical fair-share allocation, and a time-slicing contract. As a result, we shifted the debate about how much GPU time each research project deserves from a case-by-case operational task to a transparent administrative budgeting process.

At Ai2, we manage thousands of NVIDIA H100, B200, and B300 GPUs arranged in clusters ranging in size from 88 to 1024 GPUs. These clusters are built for large-scale distributed training of AI models, and they serve a group of about 150 internal researchers whose work covers a diverse set of AI domains, including the full model flow of LLM and VLM training, robotics reinforcement learning (RL) simulation, and post-training for scientific agentic use cases.

Like many labs, we have demand for GPU time that far exceeds supply. Based on submitted workloads, at any moment in time we have outstanding requests for 2-3x more GPUs than are available. One way to think about this is that every available GPU hour on our cluster has 2-3 different research workloads competing for it.

Historically, we used a priority-based scheduler, and we allowed workloads to opt out of preemptability. Each team had a limit on concurrent GPUs that could be used by workloads which were protected from preemption. Preemptible workloads could exceed that limit on idle GPUs. This strategy produced predictable pathologies. For example, we observed instances of GPU “squatting” where users would park no-op workloads they could connect to when the need arose. This occurred because researchers found they could not launch debugging workloads with low enough latency to tackle problems in real time. We also observed priority inflation, where eventually 100% of scheduled workloads used HIGH priority. This meant that lower priority levels were starved of GPU time altogether. Since preemptability was optional, we also found that our on-call engineers spent a majority of their ticket response time negotiating the organized shutdown of non-preemptable workloads running on hosts with known maintenance problems.

When these problems emerged, we were slow to identify their root causes. Our initial attempts to ensure the most important work received GPU time were focused on tighter control of how priorities were set, and, ultimately, working around the priority-based scheduler by explicitly assigning GPU monopolies to important projects. While we didn’t recognize it at first, we had built a perfect laboratory for observing the “tragedy of the commons.” Individuals were competing over a scarce, shared resource and, by seeking to maximize individual outcomes, achieving a non-optimal global result and abusing the underlying resource.

We were far from the first to observe this kind of interaction. Resource allocation is a fascinating research domain that mixes algorithm development, economics, and system management. A central problem is that users often know the value of their own jobs better than the organization does, but they may have incentives to hide that value or hold on to resources even when doing so hurts total performance. For example, in their 2011 paper introducing Dominant Resource Fairness, Ghodsi et al. recount an anecdote in which a search company provided dedicated machines to jobs only if their users could guarantee high utilization. They soon discovered “users would sprinkle their code with infinite loops to artificially inflate utilization levels.” The hardware changes, but the fundamental problems that make resource allocation complex persist.

The classic solution to a tragedy of the commons is to privatize the shared resource—owners are incentivized to maximize the value of their property. When we assigned teams monopolies over sets of GPUs, we were already doing a version of this, but it was too coarse. It caused GPUs to sit idle due to the seasonality of research. Teams are ready to run experiments and training at different times, so assigning a monopoly would ensure that there would be times when no jobs were ready to execute, with another team left waiting for capacity.

We were manually solving a knapsack problem, trying to fit dynamically changing research needs into a static schedule. We wanted the ownership incentive, but we also wanted to maintain full occupancy of the GPUs.

We decided to iterate on the ownership model. Instead of issuing teams GPUs, we chose to allocate a portion of GPU time. Predicting demand into the future would require knowing the result of novel science experiments, so it cannot be forecast with precision. Priority across research efforts, however, is a question of strategy, and it can be more easily debated and decided in advance. Instead of trying to solve the scheduling puzzle, we enabled leadership to think like investors. Before the workloads exist, decide how to fund each research effort with GPU time based on their judgment of its likely impact. The scheduler could then use that information when prioritizing arriving workloads.

With this in mind, we devised a hierarchical system where managers could proportionally allocate GPU time to the projects and researchers they were responsible for. As the diagram below illustrates, this translates program strategy directly into a guaranteed share of GPU time. Project A1 knows it has a 35% claim on total capacity, regardless of how many other projects are queuing up elsewhere.

Parenthetical values represent the total cluster capacity assigned to a leaf project.

In this system, every request for GPU time must be funded by a budget, or it is not protected from preemption. In the old system, HIGH priority carried no cost and non-preemptibility allowed a team to fill their concurrent GPU limit indefinitely, so everyone used them. Now, nothing is free, so any trick to get GPU time draws from the benefiting user’s allocation. A squatting workload is spending team budget on nothing. Our strategy is to make gaming the scheduler more expensive than honestly engaging in the debate for a larger budget. We are constantly iterating on this budget review process, but the key requirements are that there are frequent opportunities for researchers to advocate for the time they need, and the decisions are made by managers with the most context on the tradeoffs in question. This means allocation decisions within a research project are made by a lead researcher, within a research program by a principal investigator, and across programs by a lead program manager, or by the CEO.

Paired with this GPU time budgeting tool, we built a hierarchical fair-share scheduler to manage actual occupancy of allocations throughout the program tree. The algorithm here is not new—hierarchical fair-share over a time window is part of a lineage that goes back to the Hadoop Fair Scheduler in 2009, and the same approach is in active use today in SLURM’s Fair Tree and YARN’s Fair Scheduler. What’s new for us are the inputs: the tree mirrors the research program structure, and the weights are budgets set by managers rather than static quotas.

The scheduler tracks occupancy over a sliding lookback window (we default to 7 days) and sorts workloads from under-utilized allocations above those from over-utilized allocations. This way, over a week-long time range, we can expect every group to receive their allocated GPU time as long as they are actively submitting workloads with sufficient demand.

“The new scheduler makes it feel like we have an extra 30% compute. In the old scheduler, if we had moments when we didn't need our full slot limit, that compute was basically lost. Now with the new scheduler, if that happens, we can later burst beyond our allocation limit and still see our jobs scheduled quickly and without preemption, essentially letting us reclaim that compute. Our workloads are often bursty, so this gave us a significant amount of compute back.” — Chris Clark

The scheduler distinguishes two kinds of occupancy. Allocated occupancy is time during which a workload is charged to a budget. This draws from the workload owner’s allocations, which affects the fair-share budget calculation, and these workloads are protected from preemption during their minimum runtime window. Unallocated occupancy is not charged to any budget, is unprotected from the outset, and may be preempted by any allocated request. This allows us to keep the GPUs fully occupied even when allocations don’t properly match demand and prevents teams from ever declining free GPU cycles.

An additional feature of distributed training that makes fair resource allocation difficult is that workloads can run for a very long time. Training jobs regularly run for hours, days, and sometimes even weeks. Once scheduled, a workload could remain on its assigned GPUs for a week or more, providing no opportunity for others to receive their budgeted time. This is the system property that made GPU squatting possible. It’s also what forced on-call engineers to negotiate with long-running job owners to address ongoing maintenance issues.

To address these problems, we introduced a “scheduling contract.” In exchange for access to the cluster, a workload must declare its minimum runtime, or the shortest amount of occupancy required to make meaningful progress. During this time, a workload is protected from preemption. This gives the researcher a guarantee of progress, while giving the scheduler the right to rebalance once that progress is banked, automatically re-queueing resumable workloads. Alternatively, a user can set minimum runtime to zero, which indicates that the GPU time should be unallocated. These workloads are always subject to preemption, but they’re also free in the sense that they are not charged to any budget.

The workload lifecycle follows this pattern:

Together, these agreements add time-slicing to our scheduler. Running workloads may be removed and requeued automatically, allowing fair-share to converge and disincentivizing squatting. They also let unhealthy hosts drain their workloads as they reach their minimum runtimes, so repair activities can be fully automated. This last point was more important than we realized when planning this work. It reduced repairs requiring a human-in-the-loop by 74%, which was a massive savings in on-call toil.

We know that scheduling policy changes can have unintended consequences. The zero-sum nature of the problem means that giving time to one researcher means taking away from another. Users who lose this exchange tend to look for new workarounds. Before rolling out the budget-based system, we wanted a fast way to predict where those longer wait times might arise and to test configuration knobs like the length of the lookback window or the maximum value to allow for minimum runtime (we chose 8 hours).

We built a small simulation environment that takes a set of workloads and their submission schedule as input and allows the scheduler to make preemption and GPU assignment decisions. With the knowledge of each workload’s requested number of GPUs and total runtime, the simulator could jump ahead to schedulable moments and provide analysis of queue wait times, preemption events, and distribution of GPU time across projects for many simulated days in a few seconds. We ran the simulator against both historical submission data and constructed scenarios we wanted to better understand.

One hypothesis we wanted to test involved “debug workloads.” These jobs require a small number of GPUs and a minimum runtime of 15 minutes or less, which is enough for the user to see whether a job launches successfully or crashes early due to a bug or misconfiguration. We wanted to know whether these jobs would see a shorter queue wait time than larger training workloads, which often need many GPUs and hours of runtime to make meaningful progress. Intuitively, these smaller jobs should rise to the top of the queue, since a small job can fit more places than a large one. But the precise queue latency was important. A short wait of a minute or two would unlock a new development practice, but a ten-minute wait becomes infeasible.

Our simulations required hand-built test case data, because our historical record did not contain a high enough volume of these debug-like workloads. Our results supported the hypothesis, showing p90 debug workload wait times fall from about 6 hours to only 5 minutes.

Smaller-scale simulator visualization of the baseline (left) and the new “allocations” scheduler (right). Each row is one GPU; each bar is a job, colored by parent workload with one color hue per team; hatching marks time where a job is interruptible, and a red edge marks a preemption. In the baseline, long urgent jobs are never interrupted, and fewer preemptions occur on lower-priority-level work. The new scheduler has a larger mix of colors on each GPU, illustrating occupancy rotation across teams.

With simulation results in hand, we began a cluster-by-cluster rollout at the end of July. The results we care about are whether the workloads we chose to fund received their time, whether the new system maintained full occupancy, and whether researchers could reason about the scheduler to make informed decisions.

Since rollout, we have observed users and teams consistently receiving their allocated GPU time. We count the time owed to a team as its allocation capped hour by hour at its actual demand. Over the 30-day test period, teams were delivered 98% of the GPU hours they were owed, and 13 of 15 team allocations received 95% or more with the worst case receiving 90%. Occupancy on the cluster held steady at 98% before and after the change, with demand exceeding capacity by 2-3x in both periods. 18% of delivered GPU time was unallocated, which is how we maintained high occupancy during periods when funded use cases were not ready to run.

Our simulator results proved to be directionally accurate with real outcomes overperforming our predictions. Debug workload p90 queue wait time fell from 2 hours to 30 seconds under the new scheduler, against a simulated prediction of 6 hours to 5 minutes from hand-crafted test scenarios. It’s worth noting that the smaller sample size of debug workloads in the baseline meant there was higher variance in those measurements. Queue latency in general improved as a side effect of time-slicing: on our largest H100 cluster, median queue wait time fell from 5 minutes to 24 seconds, and p90 wait time fell by about a third (from 2.8 hours to 1.8 hours).

Compared against the three problems we set out to solve:

Squatting: Short debug workloads start in under a minute, reducing the value of squatting. The cost of this behavior charges the squatter’s budget, which prevents them from receiving time when they really need it.

Priority inflation: We still allow workloads to declare priority, but it only impacts sorting within a team. Managers are incentivized to monitor priority across the group to optimize the use of their budgets.

On-call toil: Unhealthy hosts drain automatically as workloads reach minimum runtime. Repairs requiring a human-in-the-loop fell by 74%.

The learning curve was steeper than we had assumed. We rolled out the change incrementally, so in the early days researchers experienced varied behavior depending on which cluster they targeted. Furthermore, our interfaces retained some old terminology (like workload priority) whose meanings had changed. Documentation alone did not resolve the confusion. What did work was conducting live explanatory sessions, providing a forum for researchers to ask questions and for the engineering team to provide deeper descriptions of both how and why the scheduler made its prioritization decisions using real examples.

This was a key moment because it marked a pivot from an early period of frustration and folk theories to the current mode, where research groups communicate more often and more broadly about the GPU needs of their experiments. Researchers are now engaging in the budgeting discussion with clearer knowledge of the tradeoffs being made to accommodate any new request.

In addition to in-person sessions, we introduced new visualizations post-launch to give users a better sense of how closely their assigned GPU time is tracking their expected allocations and directly exposing the metric used for sorting the workload queue. This provided a simple place to look when a workload was preempted to understand why. These visualizations also helped budget owners, who could see how GPU time was being used across various projects under their management.

Example visualization of allocation usage over time.

Not every use case improved. In addition to distributed training, our researchers launch interactive sessions where they perform data analysis and test training code while they write it. In the old system, a researcher could hold such a session for up to a week. With time-slicing, they were subject to the 8-hour cap on protected runtime, after which a session becomes preemptible if it exceeds its allocation. We did not appreciate the extent to which researchers were dependent on the volatile state of these sessions. Being preempted meant waiting to secure a new session and also rebuilding their

在 Ai2 的人工智能基础设施团队，我们负责为该研究所提供 GPU 计算能力，重点面向大规模分布式训练工作负载。我们将这项工作视为一个由四项彼此递进的指标构成的金字塔。

基础是可用性：硬件处于健康状态并准备好开展工作的频率。在此之上是占用率：可用时间中分配给特定工作负载的比例。接下来是影响力：最有价值的工作负载被选中并获得资源的频率。金字塔的顶端是利用率：在一个工作负载的整个生命周期内，实际使用的 GPU 容量比例。

本文讨论的是如何提升调度决策的影响力。最近，我们用一个包含 GPU 时间预算、分层公平共享分配和时间切片契约的系统，替换了基于优先级的调度器。由此，我们将“每个研究项目应获得多少 GPU 时间”的争论，从一项需要逐案处理的运营工作，转变为透明的行政预算流程。

在 Ai2，我们管理着数千块 NVIDIA H100、B200 和 B300 GPU，这些 GPU 分布在规模从 88 块到 1024 块 GPU 不等的集群中。这些集群用于 AI 模型的大规模分布式训练，服务于约 150 名内部研究人员。他们的工作覆盖广泛的 AI 领域，包括 LLM 和 VLM 训练的完整模型流程、机器人强化学习（RL）仿真，以及面向科学智能体应用场景的后训练。

与许多实验室一样，我们对 GPU 时间的需求远远超过供应。根据已提交的工作负载，在任意时刻，我们尚未满足的 GPU 请求量都是可用 GPU 数量的 2 至 3 倍。换一种理解方式，就是集群中的每个可用 GPU 小时，都有 2 至 3 个不同的研究工作负载在争夺。

过去，我们使用基于优先级的调度器，并允许工作负载选择不接受抢占。每个团队都有一个并发 GPU 数量上限，用于保护其工作负载不被抢占。可抢占工作负载则可以在空闲 GPU 上超出这一上限。这一策略带来了可预见的问题。例如，我们发现过 GPU“占位”的情况：用户会运行一些空操作工作负载，并将其停放在那里，以便有需要时连接使用。这是因为研究人员发现，他们无法以足够低的延迟启动调试工作负载，来实时处理问题。我们还观察到了优先级膨胀：最终，100% 的已调度工作负载都使用 HIGH 优先级。这意味着较低优先级的工作负载完全无法获得 GPU 时间。由于是否允许抢占是可选的，我们还发现，值班工程师在工单响应时间中，有大部分都花在协商有组织地关闭那些运行在已知存在维护问题的主机上、且不可抢占的工作负载上。

当这些问题出现时，我们迟迟未能找出其根本原因。我们最初为确保最重要的工作获得 GPU 时间所做的尝试，集中于更严格地控制优先级的设置方式；最终，我们绕过了基于优先级的调度器，转而直接为重要项目分配 GPU 独占权。起初我们并未意识到，我们已经搭建了一个观察“公地悲剧”的完美实验室。个人都在争夺一种稀缺的共享资源，并试图最大化自身收益，结果却导致全局结果不理想，同时滥用底层资源。

我们并不是最早观察到这类互动的人。资源分配是一个颇具吸引力的研究领域，融合了算法开发、经济学和系统管理。一个核心问题在于，用户通常比组织更了解自己工作任务的价值，但他们可能有动机隐藏这种价值，或者即使占用资源会损害整体性能，仍然不愿释放资源。例如，Ghodsi 等人在 2011 年发表、介绍“主导资源公平”（Dominant Resource Fairness）的论文中，讲述了这样一个轶事：一家搜索公司只有在用户能够保证高利用率的情况下，才会为工作任务提供专用机器。该公司很快发现，“用户会在代码中加入无限循环，以人为抬高利用率水平”。硬件会发生变化，但使资源分配变得复杂的根本问题依然存在。

解决公地悲剧的经典方法，是将共享资源私有化——所有者会受到激励，去最大化其财产的价值。当我们将一组 GPU 的独占权分配给团队时，实际上已经在采用这种方法，但粒度过于粗糙。它导致 GPU 因研究工作的季节性而处于空闲状态。不同团队准备运行实验和训练的时间各不相同，因此，分配独占权必然会导致某些时段没有作业准备执行，而另一个团队却在等待容量。

我们当时是在手动解决一个背包问题，试图把动态变化的研究需求装入一份静态日程表。我们希望保留所有权激励，同时也希望维持 GPU 的满占用。

我们决定对所有权模型进行迭代。我们不再向团队发放 GPU，而是选择分配一部分 GPU 时间。要预测未来的需求，就必须知道新颖科学实验的结果，因此无法进行精确预测。然而，不同研究工作的优先级属于战略问题，更容易提前进行讨论和决定。我们没有试图解决调度难题，而是让领导层以投资者的方式进行思考：在工作负载出现之前，根据对各项研究工作可能产生的影响的判断，决定为其投入多少 GPU 时间。随后，调度器就可以在确定新到达的工作负载优先级时使用这些信息。

基于这一思路，我们设计了一个分层系统，由管理者按比例向其负责的项目和研究人员分配 GPU 时间。如下图所示，这一系统将项目战略直接转化为有保障的 GPU 时间份额。无论其他地方有多少项目排队，项目 A1 都知道自己拥有总容量 35% 的使用权。

括号中的数值表示分配给某个叶项目的集群总容量。

在该系统中，每一个GPU机时申请都必须有预算支持，否则将不受抢占保护。在旧系统中，“高优先级”无需承担任何成本，且不可抢占性允许团队无休止地占满其并发GPU配额上限，导致所有人都滥用这一机制。如今，没有什么是免费的，任何获取GPU机时的取巧手段都会扣减受益用户自身的配额。霸占计算资源的任务只会白白消耗团队预算。我们的策略是让钻调度器漏洞的代价高于坦诚争取更多预算的沟通成本。我们正在持续迭代这一预算审查流程，但核心要求是让研究人员有频繁的机会争取所需机时，并由最了解相关权衡背景的管理者做出决策。这意味着：研究项目内部的分配决策由项目主导研究员做出；研究计划内部由首席研究员（PI）决定；跨计划的决策则由首席项目经理或首席执行官（CEO）统筹。

配合这款GPU机时预算工具，我们构建了一个分层公平共享调度器，用于管理整个项目层级树中的实际配额占用。这里的算法算不上全新——基于时间窗口的分层公平共享机制可追溯至2009年的Hadoop公平调度器（Hadoop Fair Scheduler），目前SLURM的Fair Tree以及YARN的Fair Scheduler中也在广泛采用相同方案。对我们而言，创新之处在于输入端：该层级树精准映射了科研项目的组织架构，且权重是由管理者设定的预算，而非静态配额。

调度器会在一个滑动的回溯窗口（我们默认为7天）内跟踪占用情况，并将配额利用率不足的负载排在过度利用配额的负载之前。通过这种方式，在一周的时间范围内，只要各团队积极提交具有充足需求的工作负载，我们就可以确保每个组都能获得其分配到的GPU机时。

“新调度器让我们感觉额外获得了30%的算力。在旧调度器下，如果我们某些时刻不需要全部的配额槽位，那些算力基本上就被浪费掉了。现在有了新调度器，如果出现这种情况，我们可以在后续阶段突破分配限制进行突发计算，且作业依然能迅速被调度且不受抢占，这实质上让我们收回了那部分算力。我们的工作负载往往具有突发性，因此这为我们挽回了大量的算力资源。”——克里斯·克拉克（Chris Clark）

调度器区分了两种占用类型。“已分配占用”（Allocated occupancy）是指工作负载计入预算的时间。这会扣减负载所有者的配额，从而影响公平共享预算的计算，且这类工作负载在其设定的最短运行时间窗口内受抢占保护。“未分配占用”（Unallocated occupancy）则不计入任何预算，从一开始就不受抢占保护，任何有预算分配的请求都可以将其抢占。这使我们即使在配额与实际需求不完全匹配时也能保持GPU的满载运行，并防止各团队拒绝使用闲置的免费GPU算力周期。

分布式训练中增加公平资源分配难度的另一个特征是工作负载的运行周期往往极长。训练作业通常会持续数小时、数天甚至数周。一旦被调度，某个负载可能会在其分配的GPU上驻留一周甚至更长时间，导致其他人无法获得其预算内的机时。正是这一系统特性使得“GPU占坑霸占”成为可能，同时也迫使值班运维工程师必须与长周期作业的所有者进行协商，才能处理持续发生的基础设施维护问题。

为了解决这些问题，我们引入了“调度契约”（scheduling contract）。作为接入集群的交换条件，每个工作负载必须声明其“最短运行时间”（minimum runtime），即取得实质性计算进展所需的最短占用时间。在此期间，该负载受抢占保护。这为研究人员提供了进度保障，同时赋予调度器在取得该阶段性进展后进行重新平衡的权力，自动将支持恢复运行的负载重新放回队列。此外，用户也可以将最短运行时间设置为零，表示该GPU时间属于未分配占用。这些负载始终面临被抢占的可能，但从不计入任何预算的角度来看，它们是免费的。

工作负载的生命周期遵循以下模式：

综合起来，这些协议为我们的调度器引入了时间分片机制。正在运行的负载可以被自动移除并重新排队，从而推动公平共享机制走向收敛，并遏制恶意占坑行为。它们还允许处于异常状态的主机在负载达到最短运行时间后逐步排空任务，使维修操作得以完全自动化。这最后一点的重要性甚至超出了我们最初规划这项工作时的预期：它将需要人工介入的维修任务减少了74%，极大地减轻了运维值班人员的繁重负担。

我们深知调度策略的变更可能会带来意想不到的后果。该问题的零和博弈本质意味着，给一位研究人员让出时间就等于剥夺了另一位研究人员的时间。在这种资源交换中受损的用户往往会寻找新的规避手段。在推行基于预算的系统之前，我们需要一种快速的方法来预测较长等待时间可能出现在何处，并测试各项配置参数，例如回溯窗口的长度或允许设置的最短运行时间上限（我们选定了8小时）。

我们构建了一个小型仿真环境，将一组工作负载及其提交计划作为输入，并允许调度器执行抢占与GPU分配决策。在获知每个工作负载所请求的GPU数量和总运行时间后，模拟器可以在数秒内快进到可调度的时间节点，并提供对多个模拟天数内的队列等待时间、抢占事件以及各项目间GPU机时分配情况的分析。我们针对历史提交数据以及希望深入理解的自建场景分别运行了该模拟器。

我们希望验证的一个假设与“调试工作负载”（debug workloads）有关。这些作业仅需要少量GPU以及15分钟或更短的最短运行时间，这足以让用户观察作业是顺利启动还是因代码漏洞或配置错误而过早崩溃。我们希望了解这类作业的队列等待时间是否会显著短于往往需要大量GPU和数小时运行时间才能取得实质进展的大型训练负载。直观上看，由于小型作业比大型作业更容易填补各类碎片空间，这些小作业应该会优先升至队列前列。然而，精准的队列延迟至关重要：一到两分钟的短暂等待能够开创一种全新的开发模式，但若是等待十分钟，这种模式就变得不再可行。

由于我们的历史记录中没有足够多的此类调试型负载，我们的仿真采用了人工构建的测试用例数据。测试结果印证了这一假设：数据显示，90分位（p90）调试工作负载的等待时间从大约6小时骤降至仅需5分钟。

基线调度器（左）与新的“配额”（allocations）调度器（右）的小规模模拟器可视化对比。每一行代表一张 GPU；每个色条代表一个作业，根据父级工作负载着色，每个团队对应一种色相；阴影线标记作业可被中断的时间段，红框边缘标记发生了抢占。在基线调度器中，长周期的紧急作业从不被中断，且在较低优先级的工作上发生的抢占更少。新调度器在每张 GPU 上的颜色混合程度更高，展示了跨团队的算力占用轮转。

掌握了仿真模拟结果后，我们在7月底开始按集群逐步推进上线。我们关心的成效是：我们决定支持的工作负载是否获得了应有的时长、新系统是否保持了满负荷占用率，以及研究人员是否能够理解调度器的运作逻辑并据此作出合理决策。

自上线以来，我们观察到用户和团队持续稳定地获得了所分配的 GPU 时长。我们将应分配给某个团队的时长计算为其配额，并按小时根据其实际需求设置上限。在为期30天的测试期内，各团队获得了其应得 GPU 时长的98%，15个团队配额中有13个获得了95%或以上，表现最差的情况也获得了90%。集群的占用率在变更前后均稳定保持在98%，在这两个时期内，需求均超出容量2到3倍。实际交付的 GPU 时长中有18%属于未分配时长，我们正是借此在受资助用例尚未准备好运行的时期保持了高占用率。

我们的模拟器结果被证实方向准确，且实际成效超出了我们的预测。在新调度器下，调试（debug）工作负载的 p90 队列等待时间从2小时降至30秒，而针对人工设计的测试场景的模拟预测值则是从6小时降至5分钟。值得注意的是，基线环境中调试工作负载的样本量较小，意味着这些测量值存在较高的方差。作为时间分片（time-slicing）带来的附带效应，整体队列延迟均有所改善：在我们最大的 H100 集群上，中位数队列等待时间从5分钟降至24秒，p90 等待时间下降了约三分之一（从2.8小时降至1.8小时）。

与我们着手解决的三大问题对比：
“占座”（Squatting）：短周期的调试工作负载在不到一分钟内即可启动，降低了占座的价值。这种行为的成本会从占座者的预算中扣除，从而阻止他们在真正需要时获取算力时间。
优先级通胀（Priority inflation）：我们仍然允许工作负载声明优先级，但这仅影响团队内部的排序。管理者有动力去监控整个团队的优先级，以优化预算的使用。
值班苦差（On-call toil）：随着工作负载达到最短运行时间，不健康的主机将自动排空。需要人工介入的修复工作减少了74%。

学习曲线比我们预想的更陡峭。由于我们是循序渐进地推进这一变更，因此在早期阶段，研究人员根据其所使用的具体集群，体验到了不同的调度行为。此外，我们的界面保留了一些旧术语（如工作负载优先级），但其含义已经改变。仅凭文档并不能消除困惑。真正奏效的是开展实时的答疑解惑会议，为研究人员提供一个提问的论坛，并让工程团队结合实际案例深入讲解调度器做出优先级决策的机制与原因。

这是一个关键时刻，因为它标志着局面从早期的挫败感与各种道听途说的民间猜想，转向了当前的模式：各研究小组现在更频繁、更广泛地沟通其实验的 GPU 需求。研究人员在参与预算讨论时，对为了容纳新请求而做出的权衡取舍有了更加清晰的认识。

除了面对面的交流会议外，我们在上线后还引入了新的可视化图表，让用户更直观地了解其被分配的 GPU 时长与预期配额之间的契合程度，并直接展示用于对工作负载队列进行排序的指标。这为在工作负载被抢占时提供了一个简便的排查入口以弄清原因。这些可视化工具还帮助了预算负责人，使他们能够看到 GPU 时长在各自管理的各个项目中的使用分布。

图：配额使用量随时间变化的可视化示例。

并非每个使用场景都得到了改善。除了分布式训练外，我们的研究人员还会启动交互式会话，边编写边测试训练代码并进行数据分析。在旧系统中，研究人员可以保留这样的会话长达一周。采用时间分片后，他们必须遵守8小时的保护运行时间上限，超过此上限后，如果超出配额，该会话就变得可被抢占。我们此前没有充分意识到研究人员对这些会话的不稳定状态依赖有多深。被抢占不仅意味着需要等待以获取新会话，还意味着必须重新构建其

aiStories.fullContent:

Kick and TikTok say a livestream of an execution would violate their policies.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Emma Roth

YouTube, Twitch, Meta, and X aren’t saying whether they’ll allow the US government to livestream an execution on their platforms. The four companies didn’t respond to The Verge’s requests for comment after an unnamed Pentagon official said yesterday that the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of a mass shooting at a Texas military base in 2009, will be livestreamed.

Two platforms responded to The Verge’s inquiries. Jamie Favazza, a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations, pointed to the platform’s policies banning “shocking and graphic content,” including “the moment of someone’s death.” Kick, a platform known for taking a hands-off approach to content moderation, confirmed that such a livestream would violate its policies. “If this was livestreamed on KICK, it would breach our Community Guidelines,” Kick spokesperson Audrey FitzGerald writes in an emailed statement to The Verge.

Hasan is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3rd at 2PM ET. YouTube, Meta, and Twitch’s community guidelines suggest that this type of content wouldn’t be allowed on their platforms, but it’s unclear whether they would make an exception for the US government.

Meta, Twitch, and X’s community guidelines explicitly state that violent content involving death isn’t allowed, while YouTube bans content that “encourages dangerous or illegal activities that risk serious physical harm or death.” YouTube says livestreams that “feature someone holding or handling a firearm” aren’t allowed, either. Rumble, an online video platform known for hosting far-right influencers, also didn’t respond to a request for comment.

有两家平台回应了The Verge的询问。TikTok美国业务发言人杰米·法瓦扎（Jamie Favazza）指出了该平台禁止“令人震惊和血腥暴力的内容”的相关政策，其中包括“某人死亡的瞬间”。以内容审核宽松著称的平台Kick证实，此类直播将违反其政策。Kick发言人奥黛丽·菲茨杰拉德（Audrey FitzGerald）在给The Verge的电子邮件声明中写道：“如果这在KICK上进行直播，将违反我们的《社区准则》。”

aiStories.fullContent:
Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

On The Vergecast: Alexa Tablets, Googlebooks, HomePads, and other ideas.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by David Pierce

It’s gadget season, and a lot of companies are launching a lot of new products. But whether it’s Microsoft dropping a high-end laptop, Amazon shipping a fancy Android tablet, or Apple diving headlong into the smart home, the actual strategy appears to be almost always the same. All these companies believe AI assistants and agents are the future of computing, and they’re building devices that put them front and center.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay dig into all this new hardware to figure out whether any of it has the right take on AI. (Or if “the AI should run the computer” is even the right idea in the first place.) They discuss Amazon’s ambitions to be a maker of great hardware, Microsoft’s powerful new take on Surface, and even whether Googlebooks can be the AI-centric future of laptops.

After all the hardware talk, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, some talk about the Paramount / Warner acquisition and what it means for the streaming landscape, the dream of “intelligent UI,” and more.

现在正值数码硬件发布季，众多企业正密集推出大量新产品。然而，无论是微软推出高端笔记本电脑、亚马逊发售新款安卓平板，还是苹果一头扎入智能家居领域，它们背后的实际战略似乎几乎如出一辙。所有这些公司都坚信，人工智能助手和智能体（Agents）代表着计算的未来，并且它们正在打造将 AI 置于核心显要位置的硬件设备。

在本期 The Vergecast 节目中，戴维（David）与尼莱（Nilay）深入探讨了所有这些新硬件，试图探究其中是否有产品真正找准了与 AI 结合的正确方向（或者说，“让 AI 来掌管电脑”这一构想本身是否真的正确）。他们探讨了亚马逊成为顶尖硬件制造商的雄心、微软对 Surface 的强劲重塑，甚至还讨论了 Googlebook 是否会成为笔记本电脑以 AI 为核心的未来形态。

aiStories.title: Automattic在董事会改组仅数周后失去代理首席财务官
aiStories.originalTitle: Automattic loses its interim CFO just weeks after boardroom shakeup
aiStories.snippet: Automattic's interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left the company less than a month after taking the role, TechCrunch has learned. Sources say his departure followed a demotion back to his previous position, marking another executive exit amid the organization's leadership turmoil.
aiStories.fullContent:
Automattic’s interim chief financial officer Jeremy Klaperman has left his position after less than a month, TechCrunch has learned. Klaperman had been elevated to the new job last month after the governance crisis at the WordPress.com parent company, which saw its entire board either quit or be fired.

The company confirmed the departure with the following statement, shared by Automattic’s director of communications Megan Fox: “Automattic will always be grateful for Jeremy Klaperman’s leadership. We wish him the best of luck on his next endeavor.”

Before serving as the organization’s interim finance chief, Klaperman had served as the CFO of Automattic’s VIP Enterprise business unit.

He had replaced the former CFO, Mark Davies, who had briefly become Automattic’s CFO after the company’s board members voted to put CEO Matt Mullenweg on leave in September. Within 33 hours of the board’s decision, Mullenweg retook the CEO role, and the board was wiped clean.

Automattic’s chief legal officer Andy Missan had also left the company alongside Davies. Both executives had signed reciprocal severance deals during Mullenweg’s short leave of absence, TechCrunch previously reported. Automattic’s new board of directors was announced in late September, and includes best-selling science-fiction author Hugh Howey; two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, Henry Khachatryan and Krutal Desai; plus author Amy Chan.

It’s unclear why Klaperman chose to leave Automattic, but sources told TechCrunch that the decision came after he was demoted back to his original role at VIP. (As an interim CFO, he could have been replaced by a permanent hire, but nothing on that front has yet to be announced.) Automattic’s spokesperson did not comment on the reason for Klaperman’s departure.

When Mullenweg originally announced Klaperman’s new role as interim CFO on Automattic’s Slack, Mullenweg reiterated that he had “100% confidence” in the company’s cash and financial position.

Automattic通过其传播总监Megan Fox发表了以下声明，确认了这一离职消息：“Automattic将始终感谢Jeremy Klaperman的领导。我们祝愿他在下一段事业中一切顺利。”

目前尚不清楚Klaperman为何选择离开Automattic，但消息人士告诉TechCrunch，这一决定是在他被降回VIP部门原职之后作出的。（作为代理首席财务官，他本可以由一名正式任命的人选替代，但目前尚未宣布相关安排。）Automattic发言人没有就Klaperman离职的原因发表评论。

aiStories.originalTitle: Beyond TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: The Side Events, Parties & Networking You Can’t Miss
aiStories.snippet: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 is just the beginning. From exclusive networking events and startup showcases to happy hours, dinners, and after-hours meetups, discover what’s happening across San Francisco during Disrupt Week, October 10–16. Find your next connection, your next opportunity, or your next favorite event.
aiStories.fullContent:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 brings founders, investors, operators, builders, and technology leaders to San Francisco from October 13-15. But the activity doesn’t stop when the conference floor closes.

Throughout Disrupt Week, startups and organizations from across the global tech ecosystem will host networking events, happy hours, showcases, demos, dinners, and more.

Here’s what’s happening around San Francisco from Saturday, October 10 through Friday, October 16.

Hosted by Polish Investment and Trade Agency (PAIH) and Upper Silesian Fund

Join us aboard the Historic Klamath for an evening connecting Poland’s innovation ecosystem with Silicon Valley during TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. Meet Polish founders, investors, technology leaders, and ecosystem partners for a discussion followed by informal networking on the San Francisco waterfront.

Hosted by Innovation Norway & Royal Norwegian Consulate General in San Francisco

An evening of fintech, global growth, and great conversations, celebrating Aparta’s selection for TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200.

Hosted by Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB)

Pak-US Tech Connect brings together Pakistani technology companies, U.S. businesses, industry leaders, investors, partners, and ecosystem stakeholders to explore opportunities for business collaboration, technology partnerships, outsourcing, investment, and market expansion.

9:00 a.m. – 11:00 a.m.

Hosted by PrincipiumX

Learn how to use first-principles thinking to uncover overlooked customer needs, differentiate your product, strengthen product-market fit, and identify opportunities for significant growth through a real-world case study.

5:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

Meet AI Barmen, a robotic bartender that creates personalized cocktails and mocktails through an interactive happy hour experience.

2:00 p.m. – 5:00 p.m.

Hosted by EPIC Connector Pte. Ltd.

Ten early-stage startups pitch their products and competitive moats to a hand-selected group of venture investors, followed by an open networking after-party.

6:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Hosted by Granite Landings LLC

Join an international startup community for an evening of food, drinks, and networking designed to build better business relationships.

6:00 p.m. – 8:00 p.m.

The Partnership Exchange turns one evening into a live deal floor for founders who know partnerships drive growth. Walk in with your company, walk out with a real hit list. The onSpark team runs Hit List Live on the spot, mapping the exact partners who can move your revenue this year, then matching you with founders in the room who belong on each other’s lists.

Every attendee gets featured in One Golden Nugget, the co-published spotlight series from Disrupt Week.

5:00 p.m. – 7:00 p.m.

SaaS founders, developers, and technical leaders can compare notes on embedded payments, monetization, and scaling beyond basic payment infrastructure over Ping-Pong, food, and drinks.

5:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Hosted by Ontology of Value

Explore work tech, robotics, and agentic AI through startup pitches, hands-on demos, and networking with founders, operators, and investors shaping the future of work.

Connect with founders, engineers, and operators building robotics, chips, rockets, and other frontier hardware over drinks and light bites in a casual setting.

7:00 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

Hosted by Khwajalabs

A live game show turns the job hunt into networking: compete using your real résumé, pitch yourself onstage, and let the audience decide who advances.

Hosted by Enterprise Ireland

Meet and mingle with Ireland’s hottest startups. Enterprise Ireland is back at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 and will welcome old friends and new faces to The Irish Shark Tank at Ireland House for happy hour. Availability is limited.

Hosted by SafetyWing

Meet founders and HR leaders over drinks while connecting with SafetyWing and discussing the challenges of navigating health benefits for startups and their teams.

5:30 p.m. – 7:30 p.m.

Hosted by EQUITY X INVESTMENTS, LLC

An invite-only gathering for AI founders and accredited investors featuring drinks, direct introductions, and informal conversations with no pitches or panels.

Hosted by Harvard Kenneth C. Griffin Graduate School of Arts and Sciences

Connect with Harvard Griffin GSAS alumni living and working in the Bay Area during an informal networking reception. Guests are welcome.

Hosted by American South Asian Network

Connect with South Asian founders, investors, operators, creators, and technology leaders through curated introductions and informal networking.

5:30 p.m. – 6:30 p.m.

Hosted by Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs

Discover how Taiwan, a powerhouse behind the global AI revolution, is bringing AI into the real world through robotics, intelligent hardware, and advanced manufacturing, with startup pitches, investor connections, and networking over light fare and drinks.

5:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

Join AI founders, security leaders, and operators for food, drinks, and conversation around social engineering, deepfakes, prompt injection, and emerging AI security threats.

Hosted by Founder-Led Media

Founders and creators building in public come together to share practical lessons on content, hooks, distribution, and growing a founder-led audience.

Step away from the conference crowd for an informal evening with founders, investors, operators, builders, creators, and the pets that make San Francisco’s startup community more human.

Hosted by WayFounder

Meet 18 emerging Korean startups through quick founder introductions, curated conversations, and open networking with investors, operators, corporate leaders, and entrepreneurs.

Connect with founders, revenue leaders, and executives working across go-to-market, partnerships, distribution, and technology while building relationships across the Bay Area startup ecosystem.

7:00 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Meet 10 startups from the Shinhan Square Bridge Global program in an intimate evening of founder conversations, networking, food, and drinks.

An invitation-only gathering bringing together Israeli founders, investors, technology executives, and strategic partners from across the Bay Area.

Join founders, operators, and AI-focused investors for a curated rooftop evening centered on networking, food, drinks, and conversations around AI and infrastructure.

5:15 p.m. – 7:15 p.m.

Hosted by Love Soul AI

The event takes place on the patio at Per Diem, beneath Salesforce Park and a short distance from Moscone West. Connect with fellow founders, investors, and members of the tech community while experiencing Love Soul AI’s hologram technology and enjoying superfood-inspired appetizers. All ages are welcome. Ticket required.

5:30 p.m. – 9:00 p.m.

Hosted by KOTRA Silicon Valley

Connect Korean startups entering the U.S. market with investors, founders, corporate partners, and Bay Area ecosystem leaders for conversations around investment, partnerships, and business opportunities.

Hosted by Peak XV Partners

Peak XV brings founders, operators, and investors together for an informal evening of drinks and conversation. No pitches required.

Hosted by Augment and Mintz

A private markets cocktail gathering with drinks, light bites, and informal conversation among founders, investors, and technology leaders.

Hosted by Improbable

See business automation happen live as Bolter turns attendees’ most dreaded weekly processes into working automations during dinner, using plain-language descriptions instead of code.

5:30 p.m. – 8:45 p.m.

Hosted by Polish Investment and Trade Agency and Upper Silesian Fund

6:00 p.m. – 10:00 p.m.

Hosted by INNOVA × BeGlobe PR Agency

Join a private rooftop gathering built for tech builders, deep tech innovators, and investors for conversations over a shared meal. No standing around, no pitch decks — just real talk and a great view.

6:00 p.m. – 11:00 p.m.

Explore physical AI, spatial intelligence, robotics, and world models through live 4D capture, demos, and conversations with founders, researchers, and investors.

Hosted by Backblaze and Flamethrower

Wind down after Disrupt with cocktails, food, and informal conversations among founders, builders, investors, and friends. No panels or presentations.

Connect with founders, engineers, investors, and design leaders building in robotics, wearables, connected devices, medtech, and other areas of hard tech.

Hosted by Hellyeah AI

Founders, investors, engineers, and operators explore how AI companies turn inference costs into business value through pricing, routing, reliability, and token-level economics.

Bring together security, privacy, and identity leaders for food, cocktails, friendly competition, and conversations about managing sensitive data and identity as AI systems become more autonomous.

6:30 p.m. – 8:30 p.m.

Explore how founders, investors, and operators can identify meaningful talent signals when AI has made résumés, profiles, and interview answers increasingly polished.

6:30 p.m. – 9:30 p.m.

Play SQLDoom deathmatch against the CedarDB team alongside arcade games, food, drinks, and conversations with database engineers and startup founders.

7:00 p.m. – 11:00 p.m.

Hosted by SignalFire

Spend the evening with founders, investors, journalists, and builders at an arts campus featuring live music, immersive art and technology, food, and drinks.

Hosted by NachoNacho

A rooftop happy hour for SaaS and AI founders, C-suite leaders, investors, and tech media. Attendance is screened and limited to approved guests.

Join a curated group of venture and corporate investors for an intimate evening with Korean founders from 14 emerging tech startups over food and wine at a private members’ club in San Francisco’s Financial District. Curated guest list. Limited capacity. Approval required.

Hosted by Fynex and Orion VC

Fynex and Orion VC host a rooftop gathering for AI founders, operators, and investors focused on AI and infrastructure. The guest list is curated to make the room itself part of the experience.

Hosted by Founder Institute

An intimate networking evening for LPs, GPs, and funded founders focused on technology, venture capital, and new relationships.

Korean startups entering the U.S. market come together with investors, founders, corporate partners, and Bay Area ecosystem leaders for an evening of casual networking and meaningful connections around potential investment, partnership, and business opportunities. Registration is required.

Hosted by 500 Global

Meet 12 Japanese startups building for global markets across AI, enterprise software, health, biotech, defense, agtech, sports tech, and consumer technology, with live demos and direct conversations with founders.

Hosted by TechEmbassy

Ten selected startups. Fast-paced pitches. Startup prizes. Venture Night brings founders, investors, and tech leaders together for a live pitch competition and Q&A, followed by a Founder Feedback Session, awards, and networking.

10:00 a.m. – 2:00 p.m.

10:00 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

Start the day with a casual waterfront run along the Embarcadero, complete with startup-themed “runway” markers, followed by coffee and networking at the Ferry Building.

4:00 p.m. – 6:00 p.m.

Hosted by Press Club

Combine sauna and cold-plunge experiences with conversations and networking around startups competing in this year’s Startup Battlefield 200. Space is limited.

Hosted by Startup Oasis

Hear startup pitches and then join breakout groups where attendees can offer feedback, make connections, or explore opportunities to work with the presenting teams.

Event details, availability and registration requirements are subject to change. Check each event’s RSVP page for the latest information before attending.

When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

aiStories.fullTranslation:
TechCrunch Disrupt 2026将于10月13日至15日在旧金山举行，届时创始人、投资者、运营者、建设者和科技行业领袖将齐聚一堂。但会议展区闭馆后，活动并不会停止。

在Disrupt周期间，来自全球科技生态系统的初创企业和机构将举办社交活动、欢乐时光、展示会、演示、晚宴等一系列活动。

以下是10月10日星期六至10月16日星期五期间旧金山各地的活动安排。

由波兰投资与贸易局（PAIH）和上西里西亚基金主办

欢迎登上历史悠久的Klamath号，在TechCrunch Disrupt 2026期间，与硅谷共同连接波兰创新生态系统。参加者将有机会结识波兰创始人、投资者、科技行业领袖和生态合作伙伴，先参加主题讨论，随后在旧金山滨水区进行非正式社交。

由挪威创新署和挪威驻旧金山总领事馆主办

这是一个围绕金融科技、全球增长和精彩交流的夜晚，庆祝Aparta入选TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 200。

由巴基斯坦软件出口委员会（PSEB）主办

Pak-US Tech Connect将汇聚巴基斯坦科技企业、美国企业、行业领袖、投资者、合作伙伴和生态系统利益相关者，共同探讨商业合作、技术伙伴关系、外包、投资和市场拓展机会。

上午9:00至11:00

由PrincipiumX主办

通过一个真实案例，学习如何运用第一性原理思维，发现被忽视的客户需求，使产品实现差异化，强化产品与市场的契合度，并识别实现显著增长的机会。

下午5:00至8:00

与AI Barmen见面。这是一名机器人调酒师，能在互动式欢乐时光体验中制作个性化鸡尾酒和无酒精鸡尾酒。

下午2:00至5:00

由EPIC Connector Pte. Ltd.主办

10家早期初创企业将向一批精心挑选的风险投资人推介产品及其竞争壁垒，随后举行开放式社交派对。

下午6:00至9:00

由Granite Landings LLC主办

加入一个国际初创企业社区，在美食、饮品和社交交流中建立更牢固的商业关系。

下午6:00至8:00

Partnership Exchange将把一个夜晚变成一个面向创始人的现场交易平台，因为他们深知合作伙伴关系能够推动增长。带着自己的公司进场，带着一份真正可执行的目标名单离场。onSpark团队将在现场开展Hit List Live，梳理出今年能够推动你营收增长的确切合作伙伴，然后将现场那些彼此应出现在对方名单上的创始人进行匹配。

每位参加者都将入选One Golden Nugget，这是Disrupt周期间联合发布的聚焦系列。

下午5:00至7:00

SaaS创始人、开发者和技术负责人可以一边打乒乓球、享用食品和饮品，一边交流嵌入式支付、变现，以及如何超越基础支付基础设施实现规模化发展。

下午5:00至9:00

由Ontology of Value主办

通过初创企业路演、亲身参与的演示，以及与塑造未来工作方式的创始人、运营者和投资者交流，探索工作科技、机器人和智能代理式人工智能。

在轻松的氛围中，边喝饮料、享用小吃，边结识正在打造机器人、芯片、火箭及其他前沿硬件的创始人、工程师和运营者。

晚上7:00至8:30

由Khwajalabs主办

一场现场游戏节目将求职转变为社交活动：参赛者使用自己的真实简历进行竞争，在舞台上推介自己，并由观众决定谁能晋级。

由爱尔兰企业局主办

与爱尔兰最具活力的初创企业见面交流。爱尔兰企业局将重返TechCrunch Disrupt 2026，在Ireland House举办欢乐时光活动，欢迎新老朋友参加“爱尔兰鲨鱼坦克”活动。名额有限。

由SafetyWing主办

与创始人和人力资源负责人一起畅饮交流，结识SafetyWing，并讨论如何应对初创企业及其团队在健康福利方面面临的挑战。

下午5:30至7:30

由EQUITY X INVESTMENTS, LLC主办

这是一场仅限受邀参加的聚会，面向人工智能创始人和合格投资者，活动包括饮品、直接引荐和非正式交流，不设路演或小组讨论。

由哈佛大学肯尼思·C·格里芬文理研究生院主办

在非正式的社交招待会上，与生活和工作在湾区的哈佛格里芬文理研究生院校友建立联系。欢迎携宾参加。

由美国南亚裔网络主办

通过精心安排的引荐和非正式社交，与南亚裔创始人、投资者、运营者、创作者和科技行业领袖建立联系。

下午5:30至6:30

由中国台湾地区经济事务主管部门主办

探索作为全球人工智能革命重要推动者的中国台湾地区，如何通过机器人、智能硬件和先进制造将人工智能应用于现实世界。活动包括初创企业路演、投资者对接，以及在享用简餐和饮品时进行社交交流。

下午5:30至8:30

与人工智能创始人、安全领域负责人和运营者一起享用美食饮品，围绕社会工程、深度伪造、提示注入和新兴人工智能安全威胁展开交流。

由Founder-Led Media主办

公开分享建设过程的创始人和创作者将聚在一起，分享有关内容、吸引眼球的开场、分发，以及如何扩大由创始人主导的受众群体等方面的实用经验。

暂时离开会议人群，在非正式的夜间活动中，与创始人、投资者、运营者、建设者、创作者，以及让旧金山初创企业社区更具人情味的宠物们交流。

由WayFounder主办

通过快速的创始人介绍、精心安排的交流，以及与投资者、运营者、企业领导者和创业者进行开放式社交，结识18家新兴韩国初创企业。

与从事市场进入、合作伙伴关系、分销和技术工作的创始人、营收负责人和高管建立联系，同时在湾区初创企业生态系统中拓展关系网络。

晚上7:00至9:00

在一个私密的夜间活动中，结识Shinhan Square Bridge Global项目的10家初创企业，与创始人交流，并享用美食和饮品。

这是一场仅限受邀参加的聚会，将汇聚来自湾区各地的以色列创始人、投资者、科技高管和战略合作伙伴。

加入创始人、运营者和专注于人工智能的投资者，参加一场精心策划的屋顶晚间活动，围绕人工智能和基础设施展开交流，并享用美食和饮品。

下午5:15至7:15

由Love Soul AI主办

活动将在Per Diem的露台举行，地点位于Salesforce Park下方，距离Moscone West不远。参加者可以结识其他创始人、投资者和科技社区成员，同时体验Love Soul AI的全息技术，并享用以超级食品为灵感的开胃小食。欢迎所有年龄段人士参加。需购票入场。

下午5:30至9:00

由韩国贸易投资促进机构硅谷办事处（KOTRA Silicon Valley）主办

与进入美国市场的韩国初创企业建立联系，并与投资者、创始人、企业合作伙伴和湾区生态系统领袖围绕投资、合作伙伴关系及商业机会展开交流。

主办方：Peak XV Partners
Peak XV 汇聚了创始人、业务运营者和投资人，共度一个轻松饮酒交流的夜晚。无需进行项目路演。

主办方：Augment 与 Mintz
一场私募市场鸡尾酒聚会，提供酒饮和小食，供创始人、投资人和科技领袖进行非正式交流。

主办方：Improbable
在晚餐期间现场见证业务自动化的发生：Bolter 将利用通俗易懂的自然语言描述而非代码，将与会者平时最头疼的每周例行流程转化为可运行的自动化程序。

下午 5:30 – 晚上 8:45
主办方：波兰投资贸易局（Polish Investment and Trade Agency）及上西里西亚基金（Upper Silesian Fund）

晚上 6:00 – 晚上 10:00
主办方：INNOVA × BeGlobe 公关机构
加入专为科技建设者、深科技创新者和投资人打造的私人屋顶聚会，在共进晚餐的同时展开交流。这里没有干站着的寒暄，也没有商业计划书路演——只有坦诚对话与迷人景致。

晚上 6:00 – 晚上 11:00
通过实时 4D 采集、现场演示以及与创始人、研究人员和投资人的对话，探索具身人工智能（physical AI）、空间智能、机器人技术和世界模型。

主办方：Backblaze 与 Flamethrower
在 Disrupt 活动后放松身心，与创始人、建设者、投资人和朋友们在鸡尾酒与美食间展开非正式交流。现场不设圆桌论坛或主题演讲。

与在机器人、可穿戴设备、联网硬件、医疗科技及其他硬科技领域深耕的创始人、工程师、投资人和设计领袖建立联系。

主办方：Hellyeah AI
创始人、投资人、工程师和运营人员共同探讨人工智能公司如何通过定价、路由调度、可靠性以及代币（token）级别经济模型，将推理成本转化为商业价值。

汇集安全、隐私和身份管理领域的领军人物，畅享美食与鸡尾酒，展开友好竞技，并探讨随着人工智能系统自主性日益提高，如何管理敏感数据和身份权限。

下午 6:30 – 晚上 8:30
探讨在人工智能让人才的简历、个人简介和面试回答日益完美修饰的当下，创始人、投资人和运营者该如何捕捉真正有价值的人才信号。

下午 6:30 – 晚上 9:30
与 CedarDB 团队进行 SQLDoom 死亡竞赛对战，同时享受街机游戏、美食、饮品，并与数据库工程师及初创公司创始人畅聊。

晚上 7:00 – 晚上 11:00
主办方：SignalFire
在充满现场音乐、沉浸式艺术与科技、美食和美酒的艺术园区，与创始人、投资人、记者和建设者共度良宵。

主办方：NachoNacho
专为 SaaS 和 AI 创始人、高管、投资人及科技媒体打造的屋顶欢乐时光酒会。参会资格经过严格筛选，仅限受邀批准的嘉宾入场。

在旧金山金融区的一家私人会员制俱乐部中，与精选的风投及企业投资人一同参加私密晚宴，品味美酒佳肴，结识来自 14 家新兴科技初创公司的韩国创始人。嘉宾名单经过精心挑选。名额有限，须经审核批准。

主办方：Fynex 与 Orion VC
Fynex 与 Orion VC 联合举办屋顶聚会，面向专注于 AI 及基础设施领域的 AI 创始人、运营者和投资人。嘉宾名单经精心甄选，让聚会人群本身成为体验的一部分。
